title: Having and not having
goal: Use *hebben*, and master the difference between *niet* and *geen* — two words for "not" that must never be swapped.
bekal: say what you have and don't have
choose *geen* or *niet* with a single question
put *niet* in the right place in the sentence
wave: Review **Unit 2**: cover the Dutch column of the jobs table, look at the English, and say each Dutch word with its *de*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bij de fietsenmaker
dialogs.intro: Budi's bike is broken. He wheels it to the repair shop at the end of the street.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Good afternoon. My bike is broken.

lines.speaker: Maker:
lines.text: Wat is er aan de hand?
lines.literal: what is there on the hand?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: De rem doet het niet. En ik heb geen licht.
lines.id: The brake doesn't work. And I have no light.
lines.literal: the brake does it not. and I have no light.

lines.speaker: Maker:
lines.text: Zonder licht mag je hier niet fietsen. Dat is een boete van vijftig euro.
lines.id: You're not allowed to cycle here without a light. That's a fifty-euro fine.
lines.literal: without light may you here not cycle. that is a fine of fifty euro.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vijftig euro? Dat heb ik niet!
lines.id: Fifty euros? I don't have that!
lines.literal: fifty euro? that have I not!

lines.speaker: Maker:
lines.text: Heeft u tijd? Het duurt een half uur.
lines.id: Do you have time? It takes half an hour.
lines.literal: have you time? it lasts a half hour.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja hoor, ik heb geen haast.
lines.literal: yes really, I have no haste.

lines.speaker: Maker:
lines.text: Mooi. Heeft u ook een slot?
lines.id: Good. Do you have a lock too?
lines.literal: nice. have you also a lock?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik heb er twee. Fietsen worden hier gestolen, hè?
lines.id: I have two. Bikes get stolen here, right?
lines.literal: I have of-them two. bikes become here stolen, eh?

lines.speaker: Maker:
lines.text: In Amsterdam wel. Hier niet zo erg.
lines.id: In Amsterdam they do. Here it's not so bad.
lines.literal: in Amsterdam indeed. here not so bad.

notes: **Wat is er aan de hand?** = "what's the matter?" A ready-made phrase; the literal meaning is no help at all.
**De rem doet het niet** — "the brake doesn't work". Dutch uses *het doet het niet* for anything that has stopped working: washing machines, lamps, computers.

**Ik heb geen licht** versus **dat heb ik niet**. Note the difference: the first negates an indefinite noun (*licht*) → *geen*; the second negates the pointing word *dat* → *niet*. The rule is in the box below.

**Zonder licht mag je hier niet fietsen** — the sentence opens with a phrase, so the verb (*mag*) jumps in front of the subject. This word-order rule gets a whole unit (Unit 10); for now, just notice the pattern.
**Hè?** at the end of a sentence = "right?" / "isn't it?". Said short with a rising tone. Don't confuse it with *hé!* (hey!), used to call someone.

**In Amsterdam wel.** — *wel* is the direct opposite of *niet*, and English has no one-word equivalent; it works like a stressed "do". It confirms what was just denied: *Ik heb geen tijd. — Ik wel.* ("I don't have time. — I do.")

**Pinnen of contant?** — *pinnen* means paying with a debit card, from the name of the PIN machine. In the Netherlands cards are far more common than cash, and some shops don't take banknotes at all. Credit cards are often refused; debit cards are what works.

grammars.title: Hebben — to have
body: Together with *zijn*, the verb *hebben* is the backbone of Dutch: later it is also used to build the past tense (Unit 17), just like English *have*.
after: In questions, *jij* still loses its *-t*: *heb je tijd?* (not *hebt je*).
Dutch uses *hebben* for bodily states where English uses "to be": *ik heb honger* (I'm hungry), *ik heb dorst* (I'm thirsty), *ik heb het koud* (I'm cold), *ik heb gelijk* (I'm right).
⚠️ *Ik ben honger* is the classic English speaker's mistake. Hunger is something you **have**, not something you **are**.

grammars.title: Geen or niet? Just one question
body: Ask yourself: **is what I'm negating a noun without a definite article?** If yes → *geen*. Anything else → *niet*.

head: Use **geen** when the noun has in front of it…
Example
rows: Ik heb **een** auto → Ik heb **geen** auto
a plural noun with no article
Ik heb kinderen → Ik heb **geen** kinderen
Ik drink koffie → Ik drink **geen** koffie

after: **Where *niet* goes** is the part most often got wrong. A practical rule: *niet* comes **after** the subject, the verb and a definite object — but **before** adjectives, prepositions and a second verb at the end of the sentence.
*Ik zie de film niet.* / *Het is niet duur.* / *Ik ga niet naar huis.* / *Ik kan niet komen.*
*Geen* always sits exactly where *een* used to be — like English *no* in "I have no car" — so its position is never a problem.

blocks.text: *Zin hebben in* (to feel like, to fancy) is used constantly and has no neat equivalent: *Heb je zin in een biertje?* = "fancy a beer?" When a verb follows, the form is *zin hebben om te …*: *Ik heb geen zin om te koken.*

blocks.title: Wel — a tiny word English doesn't have
items: As the opposite of *niet*: *Ik kom niet. — Ik wel.* (I'm not coming. — I am.)
Softening a statement: *Dat is wel goed* ≈ "yeah, that's pretty good".
Insisting on a denial: *Je hebt het niet gedaan! — Ik heb het wél gedaan!* ("I *did* do it!")
⚠️ *Wel* and *niet* never appear side by side. If you're tempted to write both, one of them is surely too many.

blocks.text: Note **dertien** and **veertien**, not *drietien* and *viertien* — both are frozen old forms, just like English *thirteen* (not *threeteen*). The rest follows a neat pattern: number + *-tien* (= *-teen*). Big numbers, prices, and the famous "backwards" system are waiting in Unit 6.
